intro: A short questionnaire, grouped into three themes. Your own impression is all we need. We go through each area properly during the session, so there are no wrong answers here.

labels.meaning: This works. Nobody loses time over it and you trust the numbers.
Workable, but it costs time, or it only works because one person knows how.
This is where things go wrong, get lost, or arrive too late to act on.
You do not do this, or it sits outside what you can see from where you work.

steps.heading: How the budget is built, and what happens once it is approved
steps.friction: Most budgets survive approval intact. What tends to break is everything after it: a version sitting in someone's inbox, a working budget rebuilt by hand, and two numbers that no longer agree.

reading.label: How to Build a Production Budget
Above the Line vs Below the Line

questions.label: Budget structure and version control
questions.hint: How budgets are built and changed, and how you know which version counts.
questions.finding: When there is no single current version, two people can be right about different numbers at the same time. Every later discussion starts with reconciling the budget instead of the production.

questions.label: A shared structure across productions
questions.hint: Whether productions start from the same structure, or everyone builds their own.
questions.finding: Without a shared structure you cannot compare productions, and every new one costs a week of rebuilding what already existed.

questions.label: Budget to production handover
questions.hint: What happens after approval, and how the people spending the money get a working budget.
questions.finding: This is the gap most tools leave open. If the working budget is rebuilt by hand after approval, it starts drifting from the approved one immediately.

questions.label: Cash flow and the funding schedule
questions.hint: Whether you can see when money actually has to be there, next to what it costs in total.
questions.finding: A production can be exactly on budget and still run out of cash in week six. Budget and funding schedule are different questions, and only one of them is usually maintained.

steps.heading: What actually gets spent, and who is allowed to commit it
steps.friction: Costs rarely arrive in the shape the budget expects. The work of making them line up is usually invisible, usually manual, and usually done by one person under time pressure.

reading.label: How Much Contingency Does a Production Need?

questions.label: Orders and committed spend
questions.hint: Whether money that is committed but not yet invoiced is visible anywhere.
questions.finding: If only invoices are visible, the budget looks healthier than it is. The overspend is already agreed, it just has not arrived yet.

questions.label: Actuals and reconciliation
questions.hint: How real costs come in, how they are coded, and how they get matched back to the budget.
questions.finding: Manual reconciliation is the most expensive habit in production finance, and the first thing to break when a production gets busy.

questions.label: Splitting costs across co-producers and funders
questions.hint: Whether costs can be attributed per partner and reported per funder without rebuilding it by hand.
questions.finding: Every partner and funder wants the numbers cut their own way. When that split lives in a separate spreadsheet, it is correct on the day it is made and drifts from that moment on.

questions.label: Approvals and controls
questions.hint: Who may commit spend, who may change a budget, and how that is recorded.
questions.finding: When approval lives in email, nobody can answer who agreed to what, and the audit happens afterwards instead of at the moment of spending.

questions.label: Handover to accounting and payroll
questions.hint: How approved costs reach your ledger and payroll systems, and how much is retyped on the way.
questions.finding: Retyping between production and accounting is where the two sets of numbers start to differ, and the difference is usually found at the wrong moment.

steps.heading: Knowing where this will land, and who gets told in time
steps.friction: A report that takes three days to build is a report about last week. The question is not only whether the numbers are right, but whether they arrive while you can still do something about them.

reading.label: What Is a Production Cost Report?

questions.label: Forecasting the final cost
questions.hint: How commitments, costs to date and remaining costs add up to an expected final cost.
questions.finding: A forecast that is refreshed once a month is a forecast you cannot steer on. The overspend is usually visible weeks before it is reported.

questions.short: working in more than one currency
questions.label: Working in more than one currency
questions.hint: Whether budgets, costs and forecasts stay comparable when money moves in another currency.
questions.finding: Rates move between the day you commit and the day you pay. If conversion happens by hand at whatever rate was to hand, the final cost becomes a moving target that nobody can explain afterwards.

questions.label: Tax incentives, rebates and grants
questions.hint: Whether what you expect back is tracked against what you actually claim and receive.
questions.finding: Incentives are budgeted as certainties and arrive as approximations. If the expected amount is not tracked against the claim, the gap surfaces after wrap.

questions.label: Reporting and visibility
questions.hint: Who gets reliable financial information, in what form, and how long it takes to produce.
questions.finding: If a report takes days to assemble, it is describing a situation that has already changed. The effort goes into producing it rather than acting on it.

questions.label: Several productions at once
questions.hint: Whether you can see across productions, not only within one of them.
questions.finding: Each production can look fine on its own while the company position is not. That only shows up when someone consolidates by hand, usually too late.

result.heading: This is what you told us
result.intro: Received, thank you. Nothing is scored here: this is your own reading of your process, and it sets the agenda for the session.
result.none_flagged: You rated everything as strong. We will spend the session looking for the smaller frictions, the ones that only show up when a production goes sideways.
next: We read your answers before we speak, so we do not spend the session on the basics.
45 minutes together, going through each area properly.
A short written summary: the three main opportunities, where the manual work sits, and what to improve first.
result.note: If Tubes can solve one of the things we find, we will show you that part. There is no obligation to continue.
